title: Selective CO2 electroreduction to C2H4 on porous Cu films synthesized by sacrificial support method
abstract: A series of copper-based electrocatalysts were prepared by the Sacrificial Support Method (SSM) with variation of synthesis parameters. Thin films of the materials were evaluated for their electrocatalytic activities towards CO2 electroreduction to short-chain (C1-C2) hydrocarbons by standard electrochemical methods. Gas-phase reaction products were quantified using an online gas chromatography system. At 0.98 V vs reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), copper oxide-derived catalysts were found to have selectivity toward C2H4 approximately one order of magnitude higher than to CH4. The highest selectivity towards C2H4 production at 0.98 V was demonstrated by the catalyst with cube morphology, synthesized with 20 wt% Cu: 80 wt% SiO2 ratio in the precursor. Possible causes for this shift in selectivity are discussed in terms of the morphology and surface/core composition as determined by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-Ray diffraction (XRD), and X-Ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). © 2017 Elsevier Ltd. sections.text:
Selective CO2 electroreduction to C2H4 on porous Cu films synthesized by sacrificial support method
Monica Padillaa, Olga Baturinab,*, Jonathan P. Gordona, Kateryna Artyushkovaa, Plamen Atanassova, Alexey Serova,* aDepartment of Chemical & Biological Engineering and Center for Micro-Engineered Materials (CMEM), The University of New Mexico, Advanced Materials Laboratory, Albuquerque, NM, 87131, USA bChemistry Division, Naval Research Laboratory, Washington D.C., 20375, USA
A R T I C L E I N F O
Article history: Received 17 December 2016 Received in revised form 3 March 2017 Accepted 7 March 2017 Available online xxx
Keywords: CO2 electroreduction Copper-based catalysts Sacrificial support method Selective electrocatalysis
A B S T R A C T
A series of copper-based electrocatalysts were prepared by the Sacrificial Support Method (SSM) with variation of synthesis parameters. Thin films of the materials were evaluated for their electrocatalytic activities towards CO2 electroreduction to short-chain (C1-C2) hydrocarbons by standard electrochemical methods. Gas-phase reaction products were quantified using an online gas chromatography system. At 0.98 V vs reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), copper oxide-derived catalysts were found to have selectivity toward C2H4 approximately one order of magnitude higher than to CH4. The highest selectivity towards C2H4 production at 0.98 V was demonstrated by the catalyst with cube morphology, synthesized with 20 wt% Cu: 80 wt% SiO2 ratio in the precursor. Possible causes for this shift in selectivity are discussed in terms of the morphology and surface/core composition as determined by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-Ray diffraction (XRD), and X-Ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS).

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Carbon dioxide (CO2) is generated in substantial quantities due to energy generating activities, accounting for 82% of the worldwide energy supply in 2014 [1]. The accumulation of atmospheric CO2 can be attributed to its unregulated and continuous release, resulting in an increase in atmospheric concentration from 278 ppm to 400 ppm since the 1850s [2]. The current concentration of CO2 strains the balance of the earth’s natural carbon cycle, resulting in acidified oceans and drastic changes in global weather patterns and motivates developments of new technologies to reduce emission rates [1,3–5]. Existing methods of reducing CO2 emissions include: increasing the percentage of energy generated from renewable or nuclear sources, utilizing CO2 capture and storage (CCS) at point sources such as power plants [6,7,8], and CO2 capture and conversion (CCC) into fuels or value added products. CCC would transform carbon emitting energy sources into carbon neutral processes by integration with intermittent renewable energy sources (e.g. solar or wind) to produce liquid or gas products, effectively
* Corresponding authors. E-mail addresses: olga.baturina@nrl.navy.mil (O. Baturina), serov@unm.edu (A. Serov
http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.jcou.2017.03.006 2212-9820/© 2017 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved.
reintroducing CO2 into the energy cycle. This has been successfully demonstrated for the selective reduction of CO2 to formic acid on Pb (94.1%) and Sn (70–80%) electrodes [9] and for syngas synthesis on alloys and Ag electrodes [10–14]. Methods of CO2 conversion include reduction in solid oxide fuel cells, reduction by metal complexes, or electrochemical reduction on metal electrodes in aqueous solutions [8,10]. The main products of CO2 reduction are small-chained carbon molecules (C1-C3) such as carbon monoxide (CO), formic acid (HCOOH), methane (CH4), ethylene (C2H4), and alcohols (CnH2n+1OH) [15–29], depending on the catalyst used, applied voltage and operating conditions. Solid-state fuel cells are currently limited to producing CO because of their high operating temperatures [8,22,30,31]. Metal complexes that have been studied are not economically viable at their current efficiencies because they contain either Pt or Pd catalytic sites [8]. Metal electrodes in aqueous media can be incorporated into established fuel cell or electrolyzer technologies, replacing cathode catalysts typically employed for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) with catalysts designed for CO2 electro-reduction (CER) while maintaining the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) at the anode
).
[8,10,11,32,33]. However, as discussed in a recent survey by Jhong et al. [34], the catalytic performance towards CER on metals in aqueous solutions is lacking, with very few available CER catalysts simultaneously exhibiting all the criteria for industrial application such as high current density, low applied voltage, durability, and selectivity towards a specific product.
Metal catalysts are categorized into four groups based on their main reduction products, as observed by Hori et al.: HCOOH (Pb, Tl, Hg, Sn, In, Cd), ii) CO (Au, Ag, Pd, Ga, Zn), iii) CH4/C2H4 (Cu), and iv) H2 (Pt, Ni, Fe, Ti) [26]. These product trends are supported by consistent, extensive observation of these categorical trends in many studies, suggesting dissimilar reaction mechanisms and/or different surface affinities for CO2 reduction intermediates [15,16,19–24,26,35–37]. The catalytic activity of metals depends not only on their intrinsic atomic properties, but also on their surface characteristics such as roughness and surface area to volume ratios, both of which affect the plane edges exposed at the surface [32,38–40].
Among metal catalysts, Cu is unique in its ability to reduce CO2 to small-chained hydrocarbons and alcohols at low temperatures and atmospheric pressures with surprisingly high conversion [25]. Since the 1980s, considerable effort has been made to elucidate the mechanism of CO2 reduction on Cu with the purpose of engineering a catalyst that would promote hydrocarbon generation from CER in aqueous solutions [21–24,38,39,41–45]. Total faradaic efficiencies of CER on Cu range from 3 to 79%, with near equal ratios of CH4 and C2H4 and varying amounts of H2 [28,46–48].
Previous studies on single and poly-crystalline Cu have revealed that CER yields are very sensitive to surface structure. Hori et al. showed increased faradaic efficiencies towards C2H4 on Cu (100) and towards CH4 on Cu (110), when compared with the products generated on Cu foil at the same potentials [38,39]. Increased faradaic efficiency towards C2H4 was also shown for the (111) surface at higher indexed facets, with Cu (711) having the highest ratio of 10:1 for selectivity of C2H4 to CH4. Another example of the effect of surface morphology is posited by Baturina et al. [46], where preferential generation of C2 species in product distribution are expected for CER on Cu nanoparticles because they are comprised of low-coordination sites and low-index facets, which are sites similar to Cu (311), Cu (511), and Cu (711) [46]. Impact of catalyst structure on selectivity is further supported by the observations of Tang et al. that Cu particles (50–100 nm) mainly yield C2H4 with minimal quantities of CH4 (faradaic efficiencies of ca. 37% and 1%, respectively) [49]. Additional studies explore the properties of oxide-derived Cu catalysts, which correlate increased activity towards CER and selectivity towards C2 products with the high CuxO:Cu00 ratios formed during catalyst synthesis [50–53]. These improvements are primarily attributed to increased surface roughness and morphologies enhanced by cubed plane edges [100], which are formed during electrochemical reduction and subsequent reordering of the catalyst surface [51–53]. Further, in a study of cubic Cu nanoparticles, the suppression of CH4 at low potentials ( 0.6 V vs. RHE) was observed and the role of surface roughness was posited to alter localized pH [54]. These examples

show how controlled morphologies of Cu nanoparticles can be designed to tune product selectivity.
The study herein presents a novel approach to synthesize unsupported, porous Cu nanoparticles with consistent and controllable morphology using a scalable sacrificial support method (SSM). With this process, the selective generation of C2H4 over CH4 can be achieved. While many of the barriers discussed remain (e.g. the CER over-potential), this study is a first step towards synthesis of scalable electrocatalysts for CO2 electroreduction to small hydrocarbon molecules.

sections.heading: 2.1. Synthesis of Cu nanoparticles
sections.text: Cu nanoparticles were produced using the sacrificial support method (SSM) [55–64]. Fumed silica (Carb-O-Sil © EH-5, 380 m2g 1) was incorporated into the minimum amount of ultrapure water (Millipore, 18 MV-cm) required to develop a well dispersed solution. Cu(NO3)2 3H2O (Sigma–Aldrich, 98.0-103%) was dissolved in ultrapure water (10 mL) and incorporated by ultrasonic force into the silica solution to form a well-mixed colloidal suspension. This solution was dried in an oven at 85 C for over 12 h. The weight percent of Cu metal to fumed silica in the precursor was varied (5, 10, 20, & 30 wt% Cu: EH-5). Particles are designated as Cu1 (5 wt%), Cu2 (10 wt%), Cu3 (20 wt%), and Cu4 (30 wt%). The dried precursor was ground into a fine powder and reduced in a hydrogen environment (100 cc min 1) up to 250 C (ramp rate: 10 C min 1) for 2 h. The reduced powders were cooled to room temperature and the reaction chamber was sealed with Parafilm© and allowed to equilibrate with an oxygen containing environment (air) for 7 d. The reduced powders were combined with a potassium hydroxide solution (7 M, KOH pellets: EMD, 85%, 25 mL) and etched for 12 h. The nanoparticles were rinsed with ultrapure water until pH neutral (pH = 7) then separated from solution using centrifugal force and dried at room temperature.

sections.heading: 2.2. Material characterization and electrochemical measurements
sections.text:
The specific surface area of the Cu nanoparticles was determined from Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) isotherm. Nitrogen absorption/desorption measurements were performed with Micrometrics Gemini BET Analyzer. The morphology of the catalysts was investigated by imaging using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Hitachi S-5200). The bulk crystal structure of the nanoparticles was studied using X-ray diffraction (XRD, Scintag Pad V, Cu anode). X-Ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were performed with a Kratos Axis Ultra DLD Xray photoelectron spectrometer using a monochromatic Al Ka source operating at 225 W. Samples inks were drop cast on a freshly cleaved mica surface and air dried before loading into the spectrometer. The data were acquired from 3 areas on the sample. Survey and high-resolution C1s, O1s, N1s, and Cu 2p were acquired at 80 and 20 eV pass energy, respectively. Standard operating conditions for charge compensation used were: bias voltage of 3.1 V, filament voltage of 1.0 V, and a filament current of 2.1 A.
Data analysis and quantification were performed using the Casa XPS software. A linear background was used for C 1s, N 1s, O 1s, and Shirley background for Cu 2p spectra. All the spectra were charge referenced to the C 1s at 284.7 eV. Quantification utilized sensitivity factors that were provided by the manufacturer. A 70% Gaussian/30% Lorentzian (GL (30)) line shape was used for the curve fittings. Due to the sensitivity of Cu00 to oxidation, samples were exposed to oxidative environments for similar durations of time prior to XRD or XPS characterization.
The electrochemical activities of the catalysts were characterized by thin-film rotating disk electrode method (RDE, Pine Wavedriver and Pine Biopotentiostat AFCBP1). Catalyst inks (0.5 mgcatmL 1) were prepared combining catalyst powders (2.0 mg) with ultrapure water (2.96 mL), isopropyl alcohol (0.74 mL), and NafionTM (0.5 wt%, 0.30 mL) and homogenized by ultrasonic force for 30 s 7.8 mL or 9.9 mL of ink was deposited on glassy carbon electrodes (Pine Instruments) with geometric surface areas of 0.196 cm2 or 0.2475 cm2, respectively, to obtain loading of 20 mgcat cm 2, and dried in air at room temperature. Electrochemical experiments were performed in a standard five neck electrochemical cell (200 mL, Pine Instruments) in either a CO2 (99.5%) or N2 saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution (prepared from granular KHCO3: Macron Chemicals, 99.7-100.5%, 100 mL) at room temperature. A Pt wire served as the counter-electrode and a Ag/ AgCl as a reference electrode (saturated KCl solution, +0.197 V vs. standard hydrogen electrode (SHE), Radiometer Analytics). For the sake of comparison, potentials vs. Ag/AgCl reference electrode were converted to RHE according to equation below:
ERHE = EAg/AgCl + E Ag/AgCl + (RT/F) pH, (1) where E Ag/AgCl is a potential of Ag/AgCl reference electrode vs. SHE, and R, T and F are universal gas constant, temperature (in K) and Faraday constant, respectively.
Catalysts thin films were stabilized by cyclic voltammetry (CV) at 100 mV s 1 prior to cycling at a scan rate of 20 mV s 1 between 0.4 and 1.4 V vs. RHE. Diffusion limitations were mitigated by rotating the working electrodes at a rate of 1600 rotations per minute (RPM). Bulk electrolysis was performed on working electrodes under the same conditions described for CVs, with potentials held constant for 1 h at 0.6, 1.0, & 1.6 V vs. RHE.
Gas phase products were quantified using a sealed RDE setup connected to a gas chromatograph (GC) [46]. Catalyst inks (5.0 mgcatmL 1) were prepared using solution ratios previously described. 13.9 mL of ink was deposited on custom-made RDE disks (surface area: 0.385 cm2, Pine Instruments) to obtain a loading of 180 mgcat cm 2. Higher loading was used in order to increase signal-to-noise ratio in GC experiments. A Pt mesh served as a counter-electrode, with a Ag/AgCl reference electrode (3 M KCl, +0.220 V vs. SHE, BASi) in a CO2 saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution (150 mL). Bulk electrolysis was performed on working electrodes under the same conditions described previously, with potentials held constant at 0.98 & 1.38 V vs. RHE for durations of more than 1 h. While holding the cell at a given potential, the gas flow from the cell was sampled at 5, 25, 45 and 65 min. Online analysis of gas phase products was achieved by thermal conductivity (TCD) and flame ionization detectors (FID) that were capable of quantifying H2, N2, O2, CO, CO2, CH4, C2H2, C2H4, and C2H6. CO detection was by FID, achieved by using a catalytic methanizer (Bruker). The three columns used for separation were: i) Haysep P 80/100, Carboxen 1000 60/80, and Molsieve 13 80/100. Partial current densities were calculated using Faraday’s law and calibration constants obtained by reference to a calibration mixture (100 ppm CO, 100 ppm CH4, 100 ppm C2H2, 100 ppm C2H4, 101 ppm C2H6, 0.1% N2, 0.1% O2, and balance Ar). The GC sample loop (0.5 mL) was purged for 5 min by gases exiting the electrochemical cell prior to
injection. Analysis of the effluent in the GC required a total time of 15 min.
Liquid reaction products were identified by NMR spectroscopy. Spectra were obtained from samples prepared from electrolyte solutions (0.70 mL) and phenol in D2O (54 mM, 0.35 mL) as an internal standard using a Bruker 300 mHz Avance III (5 s relaxation delay, 90 excitation pulse, 2.1 s acquisition, spectral range: 3900 Hz). Catalyst inks (5.0 mgcatmL 1) were drop-cast (1.67 mg cm 2) on carbon gas diffusion layers (3 cm2, GDL 25 BC, Sigracet1) and dried in an oven in air at 60 C. Electrolyte solutions were analyzed after continuous electrolysis for 5 h, while at working electrodes potentials of 1.0 and 1.4 V vs. RHE in a standard three neck electrochemical cell (150 mL) with a CO2 saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution (33 mL).

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
Characteristic SEM images of the Cu nanoparticles obtained by the SSM using different Cu:SiO2wt. ratios in the precursors are shown in Fig. 1. Catalysts powders exhibit very porous, sponge-like structures, with clearly distinguished differences in individual particle size. The catalyst particle widths were controlled by increasing the weight ratio of silica to metal in the catalyst precursor. During synthesis the silica served two purposes: first, it prevented agglomeration of smaller particles by physically separating them during thermal reduction, evident from the trend of increasing particle size with decreased silica; second, it resulted in an open, sponge-like structure when etched from the material. These results are consistent with other materials synthesized using the SSM [55–64]. The mean chord widths and standard deviations of the catalysts were measured from SEM images and are listed in
Table 1. The smallest particles of 21.5 6.7 nm were synthesized with the highest ratios of silica (5 wt.% Cu:95 wt.% SiO2). The resultant particles are clustered together in a highly porous matrix, displaying increased specific surface areas when compared to foils, listed in Table 1. The highest surface area of 25.1 m2/g was exhibited by the smallest particles of 21.5 6.7 nm, consistent with the presence of more voids, resultant from etched silica, and increased surface to volume ratios of smaller particles [65]. As SiO2 content decreases from 95 to 80 wt.%, particle size increases from 21.5 6.7 nm to 48.1 20.9 nm, and particle size distribution becomes broader (Fig. 2). However, further decrease in SiO2 content from 80 to 70 wt.% affects neither particle size, not particle size distribution. Particles synthesized with 95 and 90 wt.% SiO2 appear primarily spherical in shape (Fig. 1.1 and 2), whereas those synthesized with 80 wt.% appear cubic (Fig. 1.3) and 70 wt.% is a mixture of both spherical and cubic geometries (Fig. 1.4).
The bulk material composition of the nanoparticles was calculated from fitted XRD patterns using Jade 2010 (MDI) software to determine the mole percent (mol.%) of Cu, CuO, and Cu2O, see Fig. 3. While only Cu and Cu2O diffraction peaks are detected for smaller nanoparticles (curves 1 and 2), three phases (Cu, Cu2O and CuO) are present in XRD patterns of larger nanoparticles (curves 3 and 4), implying that larger nanoparticles are oxidized to a larger extent. The bulk composition of smaller nanoparticles is dominated by Cu2O (67.5 and 79.2%, Columns 1 and 2, in Table 1, respectively). For larger nanoparticles, mol% of Cu (46.4 and 51.9%, Column 3 and 4, respectively) is close to total mol% of Cu2O and CuO. These ratios suggest core-shell structure with Cu core and oxide shell. The presence of copper oxides can be explained by oxidation of Cu00:EH-5 composites obtained by thermal reduction of Cu(NO3)2 3H2O in a flow of H2 at 250 C [66–69]. As mentioned earlier, after reductive treatment in H2, Cu00:EH-5 composites were first exposed to air for 7 days, and then etched in 7 M KOH for 12 h in order to remove SiO2 filler.
Chemical speciation of the surface of fresh catalyst films revealed by XPS (Fig. 4a–b) is different from that of XRD, having about 33% of total metallic copper and Cu2O (which are not distinguishable by XPS, peak at 932–932.5 eV), with the remaining Cu present as oxides or hydroxides (peak at 935–936 eV), see Table 2. Large satellite in the area of 943 eV confirms Cu (II) presence. The difference between XRD and XPS speciation may be due to further oxidation of the surface of the films during ink preparation. From previous studies [40,43–45,47,48,52,53], oxidederived Cu films are expected to display high surface roughness
and a large number of low-coordination sites after their electrochemical reduction to Cu00 at negative potentials of CO2 electroreduction. Indeed, post-electrolysis analysis of the films held at 1.0 and 1.6 V vs. RHE for 5 h displays a drastic change in the chemistry of copper with satellite peak and a peak due to Cu (II) oxide disappearing (see Fig. 4c–d). The peak at 932-932.5 eV may be due to Cu00, Cu2O or their mixture. We speculate that Cu2O is reduced to Cu00 while holding electrode potentials greater than 0.98 V vs. RHE.
Equilibrium potentials for CO2 reduction to small organic molecules at pH 6.8 are within 200 mV from the equilibrium potential for hydrogen evolution reaction [9,46], as shown in the equations below.
CO2 (g) + 2H+ (aq) + 2e $ CO (g) + H2O (l), E00 = 0.504 V (2)
CO2 (g) + 2H+ (aq) + 2e $ HCOOH (l), E00 = 0.626 V (3)
CO2 (g) + 8H+ (aq) + 8e $ CH4 (g) + H2O (l), E00 = 0.232 V (4)
2CO2 (g) + 12H+ (aq) + 12 e $ C2H4 (g) + 4H2O (l), E00 = 0.322 V(5)
2H+ (aq) + 2e $ H2 (g), E00 = 0.401 V (6)
where E00 is the standard equilibrium potential. In practice, only CO2 reduction to HCOOH occurs close to equilibrium potential. Reactions 2, 4, and 5 require large overpotentials due to the slow kinetics of some of the reaction steps. The large reaction overpotential of CER on Cu (ca. 1.0 V) is attributed to a rate limiting step early in the proposed mechanism, which shifts the reaction potential of CER into the HER range [23,26,43,44,52,53]. Further, the dependence of product efficiencies on applied potential was observed by Hori et al., with less negative potentials predominantly generating H2 and more negative potentials generating a range of products [25]. The source of this change in product distribution was illuminated by Peterson et al. who calculated that H2 formation is likely the first step in this mechanism on Cu, but is limited by the formation of surface oxides on Cu in aqueous solutions and at potentials more positive than 0.40 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) [44]. Although adsorbed atomic hydrogen (Had) is a surface species that participates in CO2 reduction, it is hypothesized that HER occurs at a faster rate, and at less negative potentials, so the competitive occupation of active sites by adsorbed CO2 is slow and limits the availability of adsorbed CO intermediates (COad) at these potentials [25,43,44]. This is experimentally observed by the suppression of current density near this potential region during cyclic voltammetry [46]. Beyond potentials of ca. 0.8 V vs. RHE there are several different reaction pathways that are energetically possible, as evident by the simultaneous appearance of CO, CH4, C2H4, and HCOOH all seemingly sharing a rate limiting step that Hori et al. propose is the reduction and adsorption of a carbon dioxide anion radical to a COad intermediate, confirmed experimentally by the reduction of CO, not HCOO , results in similar product distribution as seen in CER. COad is thought subsequently reduced and hydrogenated to form a carbonyl group [25]. Peterson et al. calculated the free energies for possible reaction intermediates using a computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) model coupled with density functional theory (DFT) adsorption energies to proposed that an adsorbed CHO is likely a shared intermediate in the pathway to both CH4 and C2H4 [43]. After the formation of adsorbed CO (COad) at potentials less than 0.41 V vs. RHE, the additional reduction to CHOad was calculated as energetically favorable at potentials greater than 0.74 V vs. RHE. The potentials at which H2 and COad are possible energetic pathways for CER are nearly identical ( 0.40 and 0.41 V vs. RHE, respectively), but clearly the further reduction of COad has a larger energy barrier and thus explains the preferential formation of H2 at less negative potentials.
The activity of Cu nanoparticles towards CER was confirmed by rotating disk electrode (RDE) using cyclic voltammetry in CO2 saturated 0.1 M KHCO3, see Fig. 5. All catalysts exhibit a suppression of current near 1.05 V vs. RHE, previously attributed to the inhibition of the HER by adsorbed CO, with observed current densities between 0.5–3 mA cm 2, of similar magnitude but lower than the current densities previously reported for CER on high surface area Cu nanoparticles and nanofoams (5–8 mA cm 2) [47,48]. It can be ascertained that although these particles have similar porous structures, their catalytic sites are dissimilar, evident in the differences in current near this suppression region. Reduction onset appears nearly identical for all catalyst, however Cu1 (ca. 0.65 V vs. RHE) exhibits the sharpest slope and largest magnitude of current density for scanned potentials. Cu3 exhibits the largest suppression peak (ca. 1.35 to 1.15 V vs. RHE), indicating a larger rate limiting potential region for this catalyst. Recalling that Cu3 is the only catalyst with a cubic shape and that cubic nanoparticles have been previously reported with increased faradaic efficiency towards C2 products [51,54], this suppression may be due to the restriction of available catalytic sites for hydrogen evolution reaction by intermediate CER species prior to complete reduction. Cu2 and Cu4 are similar in their maximum current densities (3 mA cm 2 at 1.4 V), but differences in adsorbed intermediates can be observed between ca. 0.9 and 1.2 V vs. RHE, indicating that local catalytic sizes are unique. Because of remarkable differences in morphology, particles geometrical dimensions and surface chemical composition, Cu1, Cu2, and Cu3 were selected for further characterization by gas chromatography. Cu4was not selected due to its similarity to Cu3 in terms of particles dimensions and surface speciation. Faradaic efficiencies calculated from simultaneous electrochemical and gas chromatography measurements are listed in Table 2. Cu1, Cu2, and
Cu3 all generated H2, CO, CH4, and C2H4 at a 0.98 and 1.38 V vs. RHE. Faradaic efficiencies towards CO and H2 are comparable for all samples. At both potentials, Cu3 ranks the highest for faradaic efficiencies towards hydrocarbons (CH4 + C2H4) generation (21.9 % and 46.6 % at 0.98 V and 1.38 V vs. RHE, respectively), followed by Cu1 (14.5 % and 40.3 %) and Cu2 (15% and 28.7%). At 0.98 V, the three catalysts demonstrate high selectivity towards the C2H4 production, with the ratio of C2H4:CH4 faradaic efficiencies decreasing in the following row: Cu1 (15) < Cu3 (35.5) < Cu2 (149). The highest faradaic efficiency towards C2H4 production (21.6%) is observed for Cu3. This is likely is due to its unique cubic shape. Interestingly, the catalysts with highest ratio of C2H4: CH4 (Cu2 and Cu3) faradaic efficiencies both exhibit a 10-fold decrease in this ratio for CER at more negative potential of 1.38 V vs. RHE; a decrease from 149:1 to 13:1 for Cu2 and from 35.5:1 to 3:1 for Cu3 (CA at 0.98 and 1.38 vs. RHE, respectively). For Cu1, the ratio of faradaic efficiencies towards C2H4: CH4 are 15:1 and 9:1, at the same respective potentials. These results support previous observations that while CER to both products is possible, C2H4 formation is less favorable at higher reduction potentials due to multiple available reaction pathways [43,44,54]. The trend of greater selectively towards C2H4 observed for all catalysts at the potentials tested, along with a decrease in CO faradaic efficiencies at higher potentials, indicate that the conversion of COads to C2H4 is occurring more efficiently at more negative potentials. Possible causes for increased selectivity towards C2H4 observed during CER on the three catalysts may be attributed to the presence of (100) planes and C C bond promoting active sites, such as (711) resultant from reduced surface oxides.
While faradaic efficiencies presented in Table 3 represent average of four measurements, their change with time for a representative catalyst (Cu1) is shown in Fig. 6. It can be seen that
CH4, CO and H2 distribution was stable within 60 min. For C2H4 production, faradaic efficiency initially increased from 28 to 38% and then remained stable for the duration of the test. The initial increase in the C2H4 faradaic efficiency may be assigned to Cu surface reconstruction [70]. Another hypothesis to justify an initial increase in the C2H4 faradaic efficiency would be the reduction of Cu oxides, however the latter would affect initial efficiencies for all four gas-phase reaction products, not only C2H4, which is not a case. An additional confirmation is provided by the fact that the current vs. time curves measured during potential hold at 0.98 and 1.38 V (Fig. 7), achieved steady-state performance from the beginning of the test, i.e. no charge was consumed for reduction of copper oxides. Thus, Cu oxides were completely reduced to Cu00
during CV stabilization preceding potentiostatic hold. Liquid intermediates generated during CER on the synthesized
catalyst were determined by NMR to be extremely dilute concentrations of small chained alcohols, aldehydes and acids (C1-C3), consisting primarily of formic acid (CH2O2) as shown in Fig. 8. The method of collection, bulk electrolysis in a small volume of liquid, and the dilute product concentration necessitated that the catalyst be drop cast at a high weight loading on carbon to generate a detectable signal and therefore are not quantified in this study due to the known sensitivity of CER to surface changes, namely the use of carbon as a support. However, detection of liquid byproducts accounts for differences in faradaic efficiencies not explained by quantification of gas byproduct, and suggests further study is necessary for a more complete understanding of the reaction mechanism of this catalyst type.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text: Sacrificial Support Method was used for preparation of unsupported copper nanoparticles. The influence of experimental parameters such as loading of copper on silica, morphology and electrochemical potential on electrocatalytic activities of Cu films towards CO2 electroreduction to small hydrocarbon molecules were studied. The formed layers of oxide derived copper substantially changed the products distribution of CO2 electroreduction, with improved selectivity towards the formation of gaseous C2 production in contrast to previously reported monometallic copper particles.
